title: The Awakening
author: Kate Chopin
source: H.S. Stone & Company (1899) / EngageNY Grade 11 Edition
citation: Chopin, Kate. The Awakening. H.S. Stone & Company, 1899.

sections.heading: The Awakening (Key Chapters Selection)

epigraph.quote: The voice of the sea is seductive, never ceasing, whispering, clamoring, murmuring, inviting the soul to wander for a spell in abysses of solitude...

paragraphs: A green and yellow parrot, which hung in a cage outside the door, kept repeating over and over: 'Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi!' That is, 'Go away, go away, for heaven's sake!' It expressed the prevailing mood of the summer cottage at Grand Isle, where the breezes from the Gulf of Mexico blew warm across the verandas.

Mr. Pontellier looked at his wife Edna with an air of mild criticism. She had been swimming in the ocean with young Robert Lebrun. 'You are burnt beyond recognition,' he remarked, looking at her sun-browned hands. He looked at her as one looks at a valuable piece of personal property which has suffered some damage. Edna sat down on the cane rocker and looked toward the sea, feeling an unaccountable surge of tears.

A certain light was beginning to dawn dimly within her,—the light which, showing the way, forbids it. At that early period Edna was beginning to realize her position in the world as a human being, and to recognize her relations as an individual to the world within and about her. Mrs. Pontellier was not a 'mother-woman.' The mother-women seemed to prevail that summer at Grand Isle. They were women who idolized their children, worshiped their husbands, and esteemed it a holy privilege to efface themselves as individuals.

Edna had attempted all summer to learn to swim. A formidable fear of the water had always gripped her. But one night in August, when the moon rose brilliant over the Gulf and the sound of Madame Reisz playing Chopin on the piano filled the darkness, Edna walked down to the beach alone. She walked out into the water, and suddenly she was swimming. A feeling of exultation overtook her, as if some entirely new power had been bestowed upon her. She swam out toward the moonlit horizon, intoxicated with self-reliance, realizing that she possessed a soul that belonged entirely to herself.

When the summer ended and the Pontelliers returned to their grand mansion on Esplanade Street in New Orleans, Edna refused to resume her prescribed social routine. She abandoned her Tuesday reception days, dismissed callers, and spent hours painting in the upper atelier. When Léonce scolded her for neglecting her domestic responsibilities, Edna took off her wedding ring, flung it upon the carpet, and stamped upon it with her boot heel.

She resolved never again to belong to another person. She rented a small, modest bungalow nearby, which she dubbed the 'pigeon-house,' moving her paintings and books into it. But the society around her was unrelenting. Robert Lebrun, whom she passionately loved, fled to Mexico and later left her a parting note: 'I love you. Good-by—because I love you.' He could not conceive of an existence outside the rigid social laws of marriage and propriety.

In the end, Edna returned to Grand Isle. The cottages were closed, the beach deserted. She walked down to the edge of the Gulf, stripped off her clothes, and walked naked into the cold, welcoming surf. The voice of the sea spoke to the soul: the touch of the sea was sensuous, enfolding the body in its soft, close embrace. She swam out into the boundless waters, thinking of her childhood in Kentucky, the blue grass rippling in the wind, free and untamed forever.
